hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, elongated, and diagonally oriented structures—typically smooth, tapered, or curvilinear forms—set against a uniform background. The activating features include organic shapes like bird necks or limbs, and mechanical forms like rails, bicycle guards, or cylindrical handles. This neuron functions as a robust detector for diagonal edges and silhouettes, showing a strong invariance to contrast polarity; it activates for both dark objects on light backgrounds (e.g., black silhouettes against gray sky) and light objects on dark backgrounds (e.g., white ceramic or wood against deep shadow). Spatially, these features consistently traverse the frame diagonally or dominate a quadrant, occupying roughly 30–60% of the visual space. The color palette is predominantly monochromatic/grayscale, relying on the sharp luminance difference between the subject (black, charcoal, or bright white) and the background (light gray, white, or pitch black) to drive activation.
